draft.title: Causes of the Industrial Revolution
card: The Industrial Revolution was the shift from making goods by hand to making them with machines in factories. It began in Britain from about 1750.
Resources and money
Britain had plenty of coal and iron. Coal fuelled machines and furnaces, and iron built machines and tools. Wealthy landowners and merchants also had money to invest in factories, mines and canals.
Markets
Britain's colonies supplied raw materials such as cotton and bought British goods. This gave factory owners a large market for what they made.
Inventions
New machines, such as the improved steam engine, drove factories and pumped water from mines. They let work be done faster and on a larger scale.
draft.remember: Britain industrialised first because several things came together: resources, money, markets and new machines.

a.q: Why did Britain's supply of coal help industry grow from about 1750?
opts: It fuelled steam engines and iron furnaces
It was sold to colonies in exchange for cotton
It gave investors a way to earn profit from canals
It replaced the need for machines in factories
a.why: Coal was the fuel that powered steam engines and heated furnaces to make iron. Coal did not replace machines: factories still needed them, and coal was what ran them.
a.clue: Think about what made machines and furnaces run.

b.q: A Lancashire mill owner in the 1780s buys raw cotton from British colonies, runs steam-driven machines, and sells cloth overseas. Which cause of industry does the cloth sold overseas show best?
opts: Colonies as markets for British goods
Coal and iron as local resources
Wealthy investors paying for factories
An improved steam engine driving machines
b.why: Selling cloth to buyers abroad shows colonies acting as markets. The steam-driven machines are a different cause, inventions, and the raw cotton shows colonies as a supply, not the place where the goods were sold.
b.clue: Which part of the story is about who buys the goods?

a.best: It fuelled steam engines and iron furnaces

b.best: Colonies as markets for British goods

problems.detail: The scenario says the cloth is sold 'overseas', not to the colonies. Much British cloth went to Europe and other non-colonial buyers, yet the intended answer and the why treat selling abroad as proof of colonies acting as markets. Saying the cloth is sold to British colonies would remove the gap.
